claims.text: Adding approximately 5–10 at% Al to a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy and aging it will induce coherent gamma-prime precipitates.
The Al addition and gamma-prime-forming aging treatment will improve elevated-temperature mechanical properties relative to the alloy without Al.
The starting titanium- and nickel-primary alloy is a homogeneous solid solution without deliberately formed gamma-prime precipitates.
Each principal element in the starting alloy is between 5 and 35 at%.
An Al concentration of around 5–10 at% is an appropriate controlled addition for the intervention.
Optimized aging will promote the nucleation and growth of coherent gamma-prime precipitates in the modified alloy.
The structural mediator is a dispersion of coherent gamma-prime precipitates in the solid-solution matrix.
Coherent gamma-prime precipitates impede dislocation motion at elevated temperatures.
Impeded dislocation motion increases elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance by limiting plastic deformation.
The modified alloy will have higher elevated-temperature yield strength than the control.
The modified alloy will have better elevated-temperature creep resistance than the control.
Al content can strongly affect alloy microstructure, phase composition, and mechanical properties.
Keeping the Al addition low will promote gamma-prime formation without destabilizing the overall single-phase microstructure.
Aging temperature and duration can be selected to avoid precipitate overcoarsening and unwanted secondary phases.
The optimum Al concentration and aging parameters are not predetermined and require experimental optimization.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance, or failure to observe gamma-prime precipitates, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The baseline is defined as having no heat-treatment step designed to induce gamma-prime, whereas the experiment subjects both the Al-modified alloy and the unmodified control to the same gamma-prime-optimized aging treatment.

The hypothesis deliberately introduces a gamma-prime precipitate phase into a matrix, but the boundary simultaneously says the overall single-phase microstructure should not be destabilized. A precipitate-strengthened microstructure is intrinsically multiphase unless 'single phase' is intended to refer only to the matrix.
